title: HTTP/3: Why Your Internet Stops Stuttering ⚡
ig_caption:
How Computer Networks & Routing Work Under the Hood: HTTP/3 ⚡ Why it makes latency feel instant

• HTTP/1.1: multiple requests per connection = head-of-line blocking
• HTTP/2: multiplexing helps, but waits can still line up
• HTTP/3: runs on QUIC over UDP → less TCP handshake friction
• 0 round trips to get rolling (faster session resumption)
• Your phone ↔ network ↔ server: paths change, QUIC keeps streams alive
• No “greets the server like it’s 1996” → more modern connection migration

Practical takeaway: In interviews, explain that latency = handshake + queuing + retransmits; then say HTTP/3 cuts the handshake pain and reduces blocking.

fb_caption:
HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP) is the architecture-level fix for the “stutter” people feel when networks vary—especially under loss, mobility, or NAT quirks.

What’s happening under the hood:
- Legacy flow (HTTP/1.1–HTTP/2): TCP establishes state with strict ordering. When packets are delayed/lost, independent requests can still stall together (head-of-line blocking).
- HTTP/2 multiplexes streams, but the underlying TCP stream ordering can still serialize pain.
- HTTP/3 moves transport responsibility to QUIC:
  - QUIC is message-oriented with stream-level independence.
  - Multiplexed HTTP streams don’t block each other as easily when one stream suffers loss.
  - Connection setup and resumption are optimized to reduce perceived handshake latency.
  - Connection migration helps when client IP/paths change (mobile/Wi‑Fi↔cell transitions).

Production lessons & trade-offs:
- UDP-based transport: more firewall/NAT edge cases historically, but modern stacks are improving; observe real traffic patterns.
- Measuring matters: prioritize RUM/LB metrics for handshake time, TTFB, and retransmit rate; don’t judge only by “round trips” on paper.
- Compatibility strategy: use HTTPS + ALPN negotiation; maintain fallbacks to HTTP/2 where needed.

If you’re building systems: think of latency as a pipeline—DNS, connection establishment, TLS, congestion/queuing, and retransmissions. HTTP/3 addresses several of those layers directly.
